The Brown madtom (Noturus phaeus) is a small ictalurid catfish endemic to the upland streams of the Mississippi Embayment, where it occupies gravel and rubble riffles. Field surveys indicate that maximum recorded total length for this species reaches 15 cm [Li = 15 cm], a size that appears to be an asymptote attained only by the oldest individuals. Specimens approaching this length exhibit significant allometric broadening of the head and a deepening of the caudal peduncle. In contrast, puberty, as gauged by the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the presence of maturing oocytes in females, is achieved at a substantially smaller body size, with individuals reaching sexual maturation at 8 cm [Lp = 8 cm] total length. This size dimorphism in maturation is common among benthic stream fishes. Histological examination of preserved material collected over a five-year period confirmed that all fish above this lower length threshold possessed either developing ovaries or testes, whereas smaller individuals were consistently immature. The length-weight relationship derived from over three hundred individuals yields an asymptotic body mass of 25.4 grams [Wwi = 25.4 grams], providing a useful benchmark for assessing condition factors across populations.

At the onset of reproductive maturity, gravid females captured shortly before the spawning period were found to have a body mass averaging 3.6 grams [Wwp = 3.6 grams]. This relatively modest mass at puberty suggests a substantial allocation of somatic growth continues after maturation. The egg diameter in pre-ovulatory follicles ranged from 2.1 to 2.8 mm, values consistent with those reported for other Noturus species that deposit adhesive eggs in concealed nest cavities. The wet weight at birth, based on a newly hatched yolk-sac larva with an assumed spherical geometry, is estimated at approximately 0.0082 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0082 grams]. This minute size is typical of ictalurid fry and reflects the limited yolk reserves available for endotrophic development. Upon hatching, the alevin remains within the nest depression, absorbing its yolk sac while undergoing rapid fin differentiation. The duration of this entirely yolk-dependent phase is brief, with the transition to exogenous feeding occurring after about 8.5 days [ab = about 8.5 days] when embryos are incubated at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].

At approximately 16 °C [T = 16 °C], females produce 108 to 128 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 108 to 128 eggs per spawning event] and appear capable of producing a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], as no evidence of a second batch of vitellogenic oocytes was found in any post-spawning individual. The protracted period of nest guarding by the male, who fans the egg mass and defends against egg predators, likely precludes a second spawning bout within the same season. This annual fecundity, while modest in absolute number, is supplemented by the relatively high parental investment in egg defense. The maximum longevity for this species, estimated through otolith annulus counts from a long-term mark-recapture study, stands at 2,555 days [am = 2,555 days] for fish inhabiting a thermally stable spring-fed creek at a mean annual water temperature of 16 °C at a temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C].

Growth trajectories derived from length-frequency analysis of monthly collections indicate that the species exhibits rapid early growth during its first two summers before approaching an asymptotic size. The ultimate wet weight of 25.4 grams [Wwi = 25.4 grams] is attained only after approximately four years, with individuals adding little somatic mass thereafter. This decelerating growth pattern is typical of fish inhabiting stable, food-limited environments. The wet weight at puberty of 3.6 grams [Wwp = 3.6 grams] corresponds to approximately 14% of the ultimate body mass, a proportion intermediate among ictalurid catfishes. Comparative data from the closely related Noturus gyrinus suggest a similar relationship, although N. phaeus appears to mature at a slightly larger relative size. The pelvic fin ray ossification, which marks the completion of the larval-juvenile transition in this species, is complete by the time the individual reaches a total length of roughly 3 cm. Field observations confirm that the smallest actively feeding juveniles, captured in kick seines, already possess fully formed fin rays and are morphologically distinct from the planktonic larval phase.

The habitat preferences of Noturus phaeus are strongly linked to its life history strategy, which prioritizes steady growth and a relatively extended reproductive lifespan over high fecundity. Individuals inhabiting the cooler headwater reaches, where summer temperatures rarely exceed 20 °C, tend to exhibit slightly smaller asymptotic sizes compared to those in warmer downstream sections. The total length at puberty of 8 cm [Lp = 8 cm] appears to be a fixed threshold that is attained in the second or third summer, depending on local productivity. The maximum recorded total length of 15 cm [Li = 15 cm] has only been documented in a handful of specimens from the largest, most productive drainages. Population density estimates derived from electrofishing surveys suggest that adult densities are low, typically fewer than one fish per square meter of suitable riffle habitat. Conservation efforts should focus on maintaining the gravel substrate integrity and flow regimes that support the lengthy nest-guarding period and the successful recruitment of the fragile, newly hatched larvae that emerge weighing just 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams]. Future work should examine the potential for climate-mediated shifts in the timing of spawning relative to the optimal temperature window of 16 °C.
